questions.q: According to this lesson, what kind of question gets a faster, more useful answer from a data owner?
options: A specific decision, such as whether a particular value belongs in a field, rather than an open-ended request to "review" something
A vague open-ended request with no specifics at all
A question that requires the owner to learn the governance framework first
No questions at all — owners should never be contacted directly
questions.explain: The lesson recommends bringing data owners a specific decision to make rather than an open question, since that gets answered faster and respects their limited time.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend following up a verbal decision with a data owner in writing?
options: It protects everyone, including the owner, if the decision is questioned later
Written records are required by law in every jurisdiction
Verbal decisions are never considered valid in governance work
It allows the analyst to avoid ever speaking with the owner again
questions.explain: A written follow-up confirming what was decided and by whom protects the record if the decision is later questioned.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend giving data engineers along with a policy requirement, such as masking a field?
options: The "why" behind the rule — for example, that a field needs masking because it's classified restricted PII
No explanation at all, just the instruction to implement it
A link to an unrelated policy document with no specific guidance
A deadline with no other context
questions.explain: Giving engineers the reasoning behind a rule, not just the instruction, helps them make better implementation decisions when edge cases come up.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about treating a failed data quality check as a blame exercise?
options: It should be avoided — engineers are more likely to flag issues early if doing so doesn't trigger a hunt for someone to blame
It is the most effective way to improve data quality
It should happen automatically every time a check fails
It has no effect on whether engineers report issues
questions.explain: The lesson warns against turning failed checks into blame exercises, since that discourages engineers from surfacing issues early.

questions.q: How does this lesson recommend explaining a classification or access rule to analysts and BI developers?
options: In terms of what they can and can't actually do, such as "you can query this table, but exports are blocked" — not just a policy's tier name
By only stating the policy's internal tier label, with no further explanation
By refusing to explain any access rules to analysts
By requiring analysts to read the full governance framework before they're told anything
questions.explain: The lesson recommends framing rules in terms of concrete, actionable permissions rather than an abstract classification tier name alone.
